analysis.one_liner: Requires airlines to let passengers transfer paper tickets and stop penalizing partial use of tickets.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required airlines to let anyone transfer a paper airline ticket to another person for free, as long as the new traveler showed ID. It would also have made it illegal for airlines to charge extra fees or penalties when a passenger uses only part of a ticket they bought — for example, flying only the first half of a round trip. The Department of Transportation would have written the rules, and it would also have had to study whether electronic tickets could be made transferable too.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary air travelers gain the most. Being able to give or sell a ticket you can't use saves money for families whose plans change, and the ban on partial-use penalties protects passengers from being charged extra — or even sued by airlines in disputes over unused ticket segments — for simply not flying part of a trip they paid for. Travel agents also benefit because the bill forbids airlines from charging them extra fees when a client uses a ticket this way.

how_it_helps.text: Requires airlines to make any paper ticket transferable to another person at no cost, with basic ID verification and endorsement by both parties, so passengers whose plans change can hand off a ticket instead of losing its value [S3].

Prohibits airlines from barring a passenger from using only part of the transportation they purchased — such as flying one way instead of a round trip — and from imposing an extra fee or charge on that passenger [S3].
Also bars airlines from assessing an additional fee against a ticket agent who sold the transportation, protecting travel agents who process such bookings [S3].
Directs the Department of Transportation to issue implementing rules within 90 days and to send Congress recommendations on making electronic tickets transferable as well [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Airlines bear the cost. Currently, restrictions on ticket transfers and partial ticket use let carriers capture more revenue from passengers — transferability gives away resale value, and allowing partial use (especially on pricier one-way and last-minute fares) can undercut airlines' pricing strategies, since many cheaper tickets cost less than comparable one-way fares.

drawbacks.text: Transferring tickets could make it easier for people to resell tickets and complicate airlines' ability to manage capacity and pricing, particularly on routes where cheap tickets undercut one-way fares.

The transfer mechanism relies on paper tickets and in-person endorsement at a ticket counter, which would be impractical for many travelers, and the bill only directs the Department of Transportation to study electronic ticket transferability rather than require it [S3].

Critics of such rules argue that airfare pricing — where a cheap round trip can cost less than a one-way — depends on tying passengers to the full itinerary, and allowing partial use could push up overall fares for everyone else. This is a general policy argument, not drawn from the bill sources.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For passengers, the benefits are straightforward: no lost money on unused tickets and no penalties for changing plans. The costs fall on airlines, which would give up pricing power and ticket-transfer restrictions. The bill's main weakness is design: it addresses only paper tickets in an era moving rapidly to electronic tickets, leaving the more common e-ticket problem to a study rather than a fix.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Aviation Subcommittee, and it never advanced beyond that referral before the 107th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Gibbons introduced the bill on March 15, 2001 [S1] [S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure and then to the Subcommittee on Aviation [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — is recorded, and the Congress ended January 3, 2003 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airlines are better off because the bill died: they keep ticket-transfer restrictions, partial-use penalties, and fees on travel agents. Travelers who change plans keep bearing those costs.

for.name: Rep. Jim Gibbons
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require free ticket transfers and ban partial-use penalties

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican and both cosponsors were Democrats, so support was bipartisan, but with only three backers and no recorded opposition or votes, the partisan shape of the bill's fate cannot be determined.

industries.note: The bill would bar airlines from charging fees for partial ticket use, restrict their ability to charge extra to ticket agents, and require free ticket transfers — all practices that currently protect airline revenue from passengers who change plans.
The bill prohibits airlines from assessing additional fees on ticket agents who sold transportation that a customer used only in part.
